passage:
In the chemistry lab, Dilnaz was rinsing a pipette when a boy at the next bench said to Maria, "Go back to where you came from." A few others snorted.
Dilnaz froze. Her heart thumped, and while she searched for words the moment passed. Maria packed her bag in silence. Mr. Fernandes was at the far end of the room, writing on the board.
In the corridor Dilnaz caught up with her. "I should have said something. That wasn't okay. Are you alright?"
"I wasn't sure anyone had heard," Maria said.
"I heard. Do you want to sit together at lunch? And if you decide to tell Mr. Fernandes, I'll say what I heard."
Maria let out a slow breath. "Maybe. Lunch first."

qa.a: It happened in the chemistry lab, at the bench next to Dilnaz's.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz freeze instead of speaking up?
qa.a: She was caught off guard: her heart thumped and she was still searching for words when the moment passed.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz do if she hears a remark like that again?
qa.a: She could say plainly 'that isn't okay' right away, and keep checking on Maria afterwards, as she did in the corridor.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt when nobody spoke in the lab?
qa.a: Maria may have felt alone and unsure anyone had heard, which is why she said so, and why Dilnaz's check-in mattered to her.

grounding: A friend hesitates at a bigoted remark aimed at Maria, then makes a small stand afterwards by checking on her and offering to back her up.

passage:
Monday night. I'm still annoyed at myself. On the bus today Varun said to Ritu, 'Go back to Bihar, you people take all our seats,' and a few of them laughed. Ritu just looked out of the window. My heart was going so fast. I wanted to say something, but my mouth wouldn't open. I kept thinking, what if they turn on me. Two stops later I finally said, 'That's not okay,' kind of quietly. Varun rolled his eyes but stopped. It wasn't much. After school I messaged Ritu: 'Sorry I took so long. What he said was rubbish. You okay?' She replied, 'Honestly, you saying anything helped. Thanks.' At dinner I told Mummy. She said I'd done the right thing and helped me email Sinha ma'am tonight, since it's the third time. Tomorrow I'm sitting next to Ritu on the bus.
- Kishore

qa.q: What did Kishore finally say to Varun?
Why did Kishore hesitate to speak up?
qa.a: Kishore felt scared, heart racing, worried the group would turn on Kishore next.

qa.q: What small steps did Kishore take that mattered?
qa.a: Saying 'that's not okay', messaging Ritu afterwards, and getting an adult's help to report it.

qa.q: How did Ritu experience Kishore speaking up?
qa.a: She said it helped, so she felt less alone even though the words came late and quietly.

grounding: A diary showing a teen hesitating when a friend faces a bigoted remark, then taking a small stand and checking on her later.

passage:
Manjula: hey. about what Sunil said at the water cooler today
Manjula: the thing about not drinking after you
Darshan: it's fine
Manjula: it's not fine. I just stood there. I'm sorry
Darshan: you didn't say it
Manjula: I know but I heard it and froze. it was a disgusting caste thing and I should've said so
Darshan: honestly it's not the first time. I'm kind of used to it
Manjula: you shouldn't have to be. can I tell Coach Iyer? he'd want to know
Darshan: ...ok. if you're there too
Manjula: calling him now
Forty minutes later:
Manjula: coach says he's talking to Sunil and his parents tomorrow before practice. and he said sorry he didn't notice
Darshan: thanks for not letting it go
Manjula: next time I won't freeze

qa.q: What did Sunil say at the water cooler?
qa.a: Something about not drinking after Darshan, a caste remark.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling about standing there at the water cooler?
qa.a: Manjula felt guilty and ashamed for freezing instead of speaking up for a friend.

qa.q: Which small stand made the biggest difference here?
qa.a: Checking on Darshan that evening and, with Darshan's okay, getting Coach Iyer involved the same day.

qa.q: How does Darshan see the remark by now?
qa.a: Darshan feels worn down and 'used to it', which shows how often it has happened and why a friend's stand matters.

grounding: Shows a teen who froze when a friend faced a caste remark, then checks on the friend later and gets a coach involved.
